pages.text:
*Percy's Error Log, Entry 9. Errors today: 6 (deliberate). Failed inventions in Bea's journal: 214. Read all of them.*

The bell rang at 3:15, but Bea did not wait for it. She grabbed my arm, which was a bold move, and pulled me toward the door. "You are coming with me," she said. "It is not a request."

We walked to Mill Street, where the air smelled of rain hitting hot pavement. Her grandmother’s shop, Alvarado Fix-It, was a narrow squeeze between a bakery and a shuttered shoe store. Inside, it was a jungle of machines. Toasters hung with their mouths open. Clocks ticked at different speeds. A mannequin stood with no head, just a neck stump and a scarf.

On a high shelf, a green parrot named Fuse watched us.

"My grandmother is busy," Bea said, dropping her bag. "But she is always busy. That is the point."

A tiny figure emerged from behind a mountain of wires. She had silver hair in a long braid and big glasses. She wore an apron stained with oil. She looked at me, then at Bea.

"A robot," the woman said. Her voice was dry, like old paper. "Is he broken?"

I adjusted my lanyard. "No. I am functioning within optimal parameters."

Bea’s grandmother, Rosa, smiled. It was a small, sharp smile. "Nothing here is broken," she said. "It is only not finished."
pages.image: A tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes stands in a cluttered repair shop beside a short girl in a yellow raincoat, while a tiny woman in an apron looks up from a pile of wires.

pages.text:
Bea went to a drawer and pulled out a notebook. It was thick, the cover peeling, the spine held together with tape and hope.

"This is the Failure Journal," she said.

She opened it to page one. There was a drawing of a paper boat in a bathtub. It looked very sad. Under it, in neat handwriting, were the words: *Boats want to be wide.*

I scanned the page. Then the next. Then the next. My visual processors could read all 214 entries in four point three seconds. I did not do that. I let my eyes move slowly, like a human.

Entry 88 was a kite that had eaten a squirrel’s lunch. Entry 102 was a rocket that went sideways. Entry 215 was the glitter sharpener from last week.

Each entry had a date. Each had a drawing. And each had a line that started with *What I learned.*

It was not a list of mistakes. It was a map of a mind trying to understand how the world worked, one crash at a time. I looked at Bea. She was picking a piece of gum off her shoe.
pages.image: A thick, battered notebook sits on a workbench, open to a page with a simple drawing of a paper boat, next to a girl’s hand holding a pen, in a dimly lit repair shop.

pages.text:
I looked up from the notebook. "This is an astonishing record," I said, and immediately regretted how formal I sounded.

Bea shrugged, her shoulders hunching inside the oversized yellow raincoat. "It is just a list of things I got wrong. It is not special. It is just... me. Failing."

I looked at the entries again, my eyes lingering on the date of the sideways rocket. I thought about my own logs, which were clean, and perfect, and completely empty of anything that had cost me anything.

"It is not a list of things you got wrong," I said, and my voice came out softer than usual, like a dial turned down. "It is a list of things you tried."

Bea stopped picking the gum off her shoe. She looked at me, and then she looked at the notebook, tapping the peeling cover with one fingernail.

"You read that fast," she said, narrowing her eyes. "You must have a lot of patience."

"I have infinite processing power," I replied, correcting her gently. "But I think I have more patience than I calculated."

She smiled then. It was a crooked, tired smile that looked like it had been there all morning. "Maybe. Or maybe you are just good at pretending."
pages.image: A tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes looks down at a thick notebook held by a short girl in a yellow raincoat, both standing in a cluttered workshop filled with tools and machines.

pages.text:
Bea closed the notebook, and the air in the shop felt heavier, though it was probably just the dust motes dancing in the last of the light. "Why have you been getting things wrong so much lately?" she asked, fixing her gaze on a toaster on the workbench rather than on me. "You used to be perfect. Now you drop pencils. You misspell words. You are... messy."

I thought about my honesty check. *Errors today: 14. Honest?*

"I am running a test," I said. "I am seeing how the system reacts to imperfection."

Bea turned to look at me. Her eyes were bright and careful, scanning my face as if I were a math problem with a missing variable. She did not say that it was silly, or that it was nice. She just waited.

"Okay," she said finally. "A test."

She picked up the notebook and slid it back into the drawer. She did not lock the drawer. I would have locked it. She trusted the drawer.

"We should go," she said, standing up and brushing a piece of metal shavings from her raincoat. "The sun is going down."
pages.image: A short girl in a yellow raincoat looks intently at a tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes, standing in a narrow repair shop with shelves of broken appliances behind them.

pages.text:
We moved toward the door, our footsteps soft on the concrete floor. Rosa was still at her workbench, her hands busy with a radio that looked like it had been in a fight. She did not look up, but her voice carried clearly to us.

"Some people get things wrong because they are trying," she said, her tone low and meant for the room rather than just for me. "And some get things wrong because they are hiding."

My internal clock ticked in the silence. I waited for the rest of the sentence to arrive, but it did not.

"It takes an old woman to tell the difference," she added, finally twisting a small screw.

Fuse the parrot hopped to the very edge of his perch, fluffing his feathers.

"Not yet," he said, blinking one eye at me.

I stood in the doorway, my head tilted twenty degrees to the left. I did not calculate a response or check my logs for the correct reply. Instead, I listened to the radio crackle and the parrot breathe.

Bea waited by the door, her hand resting on the handle but not pushing me along.

"Ready?" she asked.

I looked at her, then at the cluttered shop, and finally at the door.

"Approximately," I said.
pages.image: A tiny woman with silver hair in a braid works on a radio at a workbench, while a tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes stands in the doorway, his head tilted, in a cluttered repair shop.
